stem: A well newborn has a red-orange stain in the nappy that the family thinks is blood; which finding commonly causes this in neonates?
explanation: Urate crystals in the urine commonly cause red-orange nappy staining in neonates and may be mistaken for blood, especially if the baby is dehydrated.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Correct because urate crystals can produce a red-orange discolouration in neonatal urine that is often mistaken for haematuria.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because nephritic syndrome causes true haematuria with other renal features, not the usual benign red-orange nappy stain in a well newborn.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because post-infectious glomerulonephritis is a cause of haematuria in older children, not the common neonatal explanation for red nappy staining.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because primary hypertension does not cause a red-orange nappy stain in a neonate.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome, not the typical benign red-orange discoloration seen in neonatal nappies.
